transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, yeah, so I'm here because my supervisor at the plant told me I really needed to talk to someone. It's just... I work on the production floor, right? And we have these stations, and you're supposed to stay at your station unless it's your scheduled break or whatever. But I just... I can't seem to do it. I keep leaving my seat. Like, I'll just pop up and walk away without even realizing I'm doing it until I'm halfway across the floor. 

And it's not just on the floor, it's during our shift meetings, too. Everyone else is sitting there listening to the shift lead, and I'm just up and pacing or going to grab a coffee or checking something on the bulletin board. I just can't stay put when I'm supposed to. My supervisor pulled me aside yesterday and said it's actually becoming a major safety problem because there's heavy machinery and forklifts and stuff, and you can't just have people taking off randomly. But I don't even think about it! It's like my legs just decide it's time to go before my brain even catches up. I just... I take off. And I know it's bad, I know I shouldn't, but sitting there just feels impossible sometimes. So, yeah, that's why I'm here. They said I need to get it sorted out or I might lose my job, and I really need this job, you know?

Would you say you've struggled with this kind of restlessness and trouble staying seated for as long as you can remember, even back in school, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

Oh, wow, yeah, no, this isn't new at all. It's... it's honestly been like this my whole life, as far back as I can remember. Like, even in elementary school, I was always that kid. You know, the one the teachers were always getting frustrated with? I just couldn't stay in my seat then, either. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she actually tried taping a square on the floor around my desk and told me I couldn't step outside the tape during lessons, but it didn't work. I'd just forget it was there and wander over to the pencil sharpener or go look out the window if a bird flew by or something. 

And it wasn't just the wandering around the room, either. I was always getting notes sent home to my mom because I was talking over the teacher or blurting things out. Like, I'd know the answer to a question, or I'd just have a thought pop into my head, and I couldn't hold it in. I'd just shout it out before she even called on anyone. It drove them crazy. My mom used to have this whole folder of just... bad behavior notes. "She won't sit still," "She interrupts," "She's distracting the other students." It's like my brain was just going a million miles an hour and my body was just trying to keep up. 

So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing. It was like that in middle school, too, and high school, before I dropped out. It's just... it's always been me. I guess it's just a bigger deal now because, you know, heavy machinery and losing my job and all that. But yeah, definitely since I was a little kid.

latest_inference.note: Patient reports lifelong, childhood-onset hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattentiveness (inability to stay seated, blurting answers, distractibility) persisting into adulthood, consistent with ADHD. This chronic developmental pattern rules out panic disorder (F41.1), medication/substance-induced akathisia (G25.81, G25.71), and major depressive disorder (F30.9), which do not typically present with this lifelong, pervasive presentation.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a lifelong pattern of hyperactivity and impulsivity—leaving her seat when expected to remain seated, pacing during meetings, blurting out answers, and interrupting—dating back to early elementary school and persisting into adulthood. Symptoms are present across multiple settings (school then, workplace now) and cause significant functional impairment (job jeopardy, safety concerns). No mention of significant inattentive symptoms (e.g., disorganization, forgetfulness, difficulty sustaining attention on tasks) beyond hyperactive/impulsive presentation, supporting predominantly hyperactive-impulsive subtype rather than combined type.
